blocks.text: 1. Stationarity

blocks.alt: A stationary series keeps the same mean and variance over time

blocks.text: Hidden Markov Models, covered in the Probability-Based Models module, already applied the Markov Property to sequential data, working with one specific kind of temporal structure. The Time Series Machine Learning module now turns to the broader family of techniques built specifically for temporally ordered data, and Stationarity opens this module as the single most foundational statistical property a time series can have, one that shapes nearly every decision covered throughout the rest of this module.

This directly connects back to the chronological-order discipline already emphasized throughout Time Series Split in the Cross Validation module, though stationarity addresses a genuinely different, earlier question: not how to split temporally ordered data for evaluation, but whether the data's own underlying statistical behavior is even stable enough to model reliably in the first place.
2. The Definition

A time series is called stationary if its statistical properties do not change over time. Concretely, this means the series' mean stays roughly constant, regardless of which window of time is actually examined, its variance stays roughly constant across different windows too, and the relationship between values separated by a given time lag stays roughly consistent throughout the series as well.

This is a genuinely strong requirement, and real-world time series frequently violate it in one way or another, but it is worth understanding precisely, since it is exactly the property several classical forecasting techniques covered later in this module either require directly or work considerably better when it holds at least approximately.
3. A Concrete Non-Stationary Example

blocks.alt: A rising trend is a concrete non-stationary example

blocks.text: A stock price that climbs steadily over several years offers a clear, concrete example of a non-stationary series: its mean keeps shifting upward as time passes, meaning the average price computed over an early window looks nothing like the average price computed over a later window, a direct violation of the constant-mean requirement covered in the previous section.

A genuinely stationary series, by contrast, might still wander up and down from period to period, but it consistently reverts back toward the same long-run average level, rather than drifting further and further away from wherever it started. This contrast, persistent drift away from an ever-shifting level versus wandering around a consistent, stable level, is the most intuitive, visually recognizable signature separating non-stationary from stationary behavior.
4. Why Stationarity Matters

blocks.alt: Many models genuinely assume a stationary series

blocks.text: This connects directly back to a concern already implicit throughout the Distribution Analysis topic earlier in this course: a model is only as reliable as the assumption that the data it eventually encounters resembles the data it was actually trained on. Many classical forecasting models, several of which are covered later in this Time Series Machine Learning module, explicitly assume the underlying statistical properties of the series stay constant over time.

Fitting such a model directly to genuinely non-stationary data violates that core assumption, and the direct, practical consequence is that patterns the model learned from one period of the data may simply not hold true in a later period, since the series' own underlying behavior has shifted in the meantime. This is precisely why checking for stationarity, and addressing it directly when it is absent, is one of the very first steps in nearly any serious time series modeling workflow.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Applying a stationarity-assuming model directly to non-stationary data without first checking or addressing this issue is one of the most common, avoidable mistakes in time series modeling, and it can produce forecasts that look reasonable on historical data while performing genuinely poorly going forward.

blocks.text: 5. A Simple Visual Check

The simplest, most direct first check for stationarity is also the most accessible: plot the raw time series directly and look at it. A series that wanders with no fixed center, or that drifts consistently in one direction over the plotted time range, is very likely non-stationary, exactly the pattern already illustrated in the stock price example covered earlier in this topic.

A series that instead hovers around a consistent level throughout the plotted range, with no obvious sustained upward or downward drift, is a reasonable candidate for being stationary, though this visual impression alone is not fully conclusive and is worth confirming with the more rigorous, formal statistical test covered in the next section.
6. The Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test

blocks.alt: A series runs through the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test to check stationarity

blocks.text: The Augmented Dickey-Fuller test, commonly abbreviated ADF, is the standard, formal statistical test used to check stationarity rigorously, beyond just the visual inspection covered in the previous section. Like many formal statistical tests, it works by testing a specific null hypothesis, in this case that the series is non-stationary.

A small resulting p-value provides evidence against this null hypothesis, allowing it to be rejected, and taken as reasonable statistical evidence that the series actually is stationary. A large p-value fails to reject the null hypothesis, meaning there is no strong statistical evidence against the series being non-stationary. Running this formal test, rather than relying purely on visual inspection alone, is standard, recommended practice before committing to any modeling approach that assumes stationarity.

blocks.text: 7. Differencing: A Standard Fix

blocks.alt: A non-stationary series gets differenced into a stationary one

blocks.text: When a series is identified as non-stationary through either the visual check or the formal ADF test, differencing is the standard, most common technique used to address it directly. Differencing transforms the series by subtracting each value from the value immediately preceding it, converting a series about absolute levels into a series about changes between consecutive levels instead.

This transformation very often removes trend, one of the most common specific causes of non-stationarity, covered in full depth in the very next topic, effectively converting a genuinely non-stationary series into one that behaves in a reasonably stationary way. Differencing can be applied more than once, called second-order differencing, if a single round of differencing does not fully resolve the non-stationarity, though most real time series need only one round.
8. Two Common Causes, Previewed

blocks.alt: Stationarity gets broken by trend and by seasonality

blocks.text: Two of the most common specific causes of non-stationarity deserve a brief preview here, ahead of their own full, dedicated treatment in upcoming topics. Trend, a long-term, sustained upward or downward movement in the series, exactly the pattern already illustrated in the stock price example earlier in this topic, is covered in full depth in the very next topic in this module.

Seasonality, a repeating, predictable pattern that recurs at fixed intervals, is covered in full depth two topics from now, and it directly connects back to the seasonality caveat already raised for Time Series Split in the Cross Validation module. Trend is typically removed through ordinary differencing, already covered in the previous section, or by explicitly modeling and subtracting the trend component directly. Seasonality is typically removed through seasonal differencing, subtracting a value from the value one full seasonal cycle earlier, or by explicitly modeling the seasonal pattern directly.

blocks.text: 9. A Practical Workflow

blocks.alt: Stationarity is covered here, trend comes next

blocks.text: Putting everything covered throughout this topic together into one practical, repeatable workflow: first, plot the raw series and look for obvious drift or trend visually, exactly the simple first check already covered earlier in this topic. Second, run a formal statistical test, the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test being the standard choice, to confirm or challenge that initial visual impression rigorously.

Third, if the series is found to be non-stationary, apply differencing, or another appropriate transformation, to address the specific cause identified. Fourth, re-run the formal test on the transformed series to confirm the transformation actually achieved stationarity, repeating the transform-and-retest cycle if necessary until the series passes. Only once a series has been confirmed reasonably stationary should it be handed to a stationarity-assuming forecasting technique, several of which are covered later in this module.
10. Worked Example
The example below runs the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test on both a non-stationary series with a clear trend and its differenced, stationary counterpart.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
n_points = 200

# A non-stationary series: a clear upward trend plus noise
trending_series = np.cumsum(rng.normal(loc=0.5, scale=1, size=n_points))

# A stationary series: noise fluctuating around a constant mean
stationary_series = rng.normal(loc=10, scale=1, size=n_points)

for name, series in [("Trending (non-stationary)", trending_series), ("Stationary", stationary_series)]:
    result = adfuller(series)
    print(f"{name}: ADF statistic={result[0]:.3f}, p-value={result[1]:.4f}")

# Difference the trending series and re-test
differenced = np.diff(trending_series)
result_diff = adfuller(differenced)
print(f"\nDifferenced trending series: ADF statistic={result_diff[0]:.3f}, p-value={result_diff[1]:.4f}")
print("Differencing should produce a much smaller p-value, evidence the transformed series is now stationary")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The original trending series should show a large ADF p-value, evidence of non-stationarity, while the differenced version should show a much smaller p-value, direct, numerical confirmation that differencing successfully addressed the trend-driven non-stationarity covered throughout this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Stationarity means a time series' statistical properties, mean, variance, and lag relationships, do not change over time.
A non-stationary series, like a steadily climbing stock price, has a mean that keeps shifting rather than staying stable.
Many classical forecasting models assume stationarity, and violating that assumption can produce unreliable forecasts.
A simple visual plot is the first check; the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test provides a formal, rigorous confirmation.
Differencing, subtracting each value from the one before it, is the standard technique for achieving stationarity.
Trend and seasonality are two of the most common causes of non-stationarity, each covered in full depth in upcoming topics.
A practical workflow: plot, formally test, transform if needed, then re-test before applying a stationarity-assuming model.
This foundational property shapes nearly every modeling decision covered throughout the rest of this module.
Next up: Trend, the first of the two common non-stationarity causes previewed here, covered in its own full depth.
